options: `lib swap`
Nothing
`lib swap` twice
It is ill-formed: the call is ambiguous
questions.explanation: A qualified call `std::swap(a, b)` performs no argument-dependent lookup, so the hidden friend in `lib` is never a candidate. The generic `std::swap` template exchanges the values with one move construction and two move assignments, printing nothing. To reach the custom `swap`, write `using std::swap; swap(a, b);` or call `std::ranges::swap(a, b)`.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the two marked calls is true?
options: Both compile; call 2 converts `3.0` to `Meters`
Call 1 is ill-formed because `print` is not declared at namespace scope
Call 2 is ill-formed: no argument has type `Meters`, so ADL never looks inside `geo`
Both are ill-formed, because a friend function cannot be called without qualification
questions.explanation: A friend defined only inside a class is a hidden friend: it belongs to `geo` but ordinary lookup cannot find it, and only argument-dependent lookup triggered by an argument of type `Meters` can. Call 1 has such an argument, so it works. Call 2 passes a `double`, which has no associated namespaces, so the name is not found at all and the implicit conversion is never considered. That is a deliberate benefit of hidden friends.

options: `lib swap`
Nothing: the using-declaration names an object, so ADL is switched off and `lib::swap` is never called
`lib swap` twice
It is ill-formed: the call is ambiguous between the object and the friend
questions.explanation: Ordinary lookup finds the object `std::ranges::swap`, and because it is not a function, ADL is not performed for this call, so there is no ambiguity. The object's call operator then performs its own unqualified, ADL-based lookup for `swap(t, u)`, which finds the hidden friend and prints once. The second option is right that ADL is suppressed at the call site, but misses that the customization point object does the lookup internally.

questions.prompt: What happens with the call to `find`?
options: It calls `std::find`, because the using-declaration takes priority
It calls `lib::find`, because ADL results are preferred
It calls `std::ranges::find`
It is ill-formed: the call is ambiguous between `std::find` and `lib::find`
questions.explanation: `std::find` is a function template, so ADL still runs, and `lib` is an associated namespace through the template argument `lib::Rec` of the vector's iterator type. Both templates have the same parameter pattern, neither is more specialized, and the call is ambiguous. Had the using-declaration named the niebloid `std::ranges::find`, ordinary lookup would find an object, ADL would be suppressed, and the call would be unambiguous.

options: Yes: `ranges::begin` and `ranges::end` use the members and never reach the ADL step
No: ADL finds the deleted functions, which makes `ranges::begin` ill-formed

questions.explanation: `ranges::begin` tries its strategies in order: array, then a valid member `t.begin()` returning an iterator, then ADL-only `begin(t)`. The member is valid here, so the deleted free functions are never looked at. The last option is wrong on its own terms: deleted functions do take part in overload resolution, and selecting one makes the expression invalid, which is exactly what would happen if there were no members.

questions.explanation: `ranges::swap` tries an ADL `swap`, which needs a class or enumeration argument; then `swap_ranges` for lvalue arrays of equal extent; then a move-based exchange of two lvalues of the same movable type. `int[2]` and `int[3]` fail all three, so the call operator is not viable and the call does not compile. Arrays are never swapped partially.

questions.prompt: In C++20 and later, what is the status of this explicit specialization?
options: Allowed, because it depends on a program-defined type
Ill-formed: a diagnostic is required
Allowed only if it is declared `noexcept`
Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: Since C++20 (P0551), [namespace.std] allows programs to specialize standard library class templates for program-defined types, but no longer function templates, so this declaration has undefined behavior. Until C++17 it was permitted, which is why the first option is tempting. Compilers accept it silently; put a hidden friend `swap` in the class instead.

questions.prompt: `MyType` and `MyView` are program-defined types that meet the relevant requirements. Which of these declarations has undefined behavior?
options: `template<> struct std::hash<MyType> { std::size_t operator()(const MyType&) const; };`
`template<> struct std::is_integral<MyType> : std::true_type {};`
`template<> inline constexpr bool std::ranges::enable_borrowed_range<MyView> = true;`
`template<> struct std::tuple_size<MyType> : std::integral_constant<std::size_t, 2> {};`
questions.explanation: [namespace.std] and [meta.rqmts] forbid specializing the templates in `<type_traits>`, with `common_type` and `basic_common_reference` as the only exceptions, so specializing `is_integral` is undefined behavior. `std::hash` is a class template specialized for a program-defined type, which is allowed. `enable_borrowed_range` is one of the variable templates the standard explicitly lets programs specialize for their own types. Specializing `std::tuple_size`, as for structured bindings, is an ordinary class template specialization and is allowed too.
